text.p: Nothing in this town and especially in professional boxing is quite like it seems, but Mike Tyson, this week at least, seemed to reveal a new introspection, a new sense of his peace with his place in the world.

Tyson, who will defend his World Boxing Association title against Evander Holyfield on Saturday at the MGM Grand Hotel, held court earlier this week for a group of reporters at promoter Don King's opulent home in one of the walled off private communities on the outskirts of town.
It was a remarkably relaxed, smiling and expansive Tyson, who was willing to answer questions and volunteer his thoughts on subjects ranging from politics to diapers.

It was a decided contrast to the one-line, pat responses or outright surliness he often has shown, with the prodding of his cadre of handlers who often go out of their way to spout diatribes against reporters, since his release from prison in March, 1995.
Tyson, 30, implied he had a prison epiphany triggered by a visit from the late rap musician Tupac Shakur.

Tyson was trying to tell Shakur to be more moderate in his behaviour. But Shakur, Tyson said, ranted with a string of profanities about people having to take what they want in life, that Tyson was his role model and that his conversion to Islam was a waste of time.
"So I called my friends and asked them to tell me the truth. 'Was I crazy like that? Did I say things like that?' They said, 'yeah, man. You were crazy.'
"So I said, Holy (expletive)!"

Tyson, sitting on one of King's white leather couches in front of a pool table, wearing a watch cap, t-shirt and exercise pants, gave perfunctory answers to questions about boxing other than to say if Holyfield, the underdog in the early betting, is predicting their fight will not last the scheduled 12 rounds, "I think I tend to agree with him.'
Tyson was asked how he thought Bruce Seldon felt after his embarrassing loss to Tyson in the first round in September on what most people think was a dubious knockout punch at best.
"You don't quit. Just take your beating. What the hell, what's that. It's not too bad. You keep fighting until you can't fight no more. The one thing you got is your dignity.
"That's the fraternity to take a beating like a man. Never quit. Never quit."
Politics -- he's not a Republican but agrees with some of their positions -- and raising his three daughters were subjects high in holding Tyson's interest.
Tyson said he agrees with Republicans who want to eliminate welfare.
"I think I love most of the Republican views," Tyson said. "I just hate the white, racist Republicans. I just think people shouldn't have handouts ... they take away your dignity.

"I know my friends when they read this are gonna kill me. (Welfare) takes away our dignity and our strength and our ability to fight and strive for a better way of life," said Tyson, who added that not being able to vote because he is a felon greatly bothers him.
In a discourse on old-time fighters, Tyson spoke about writers like Jack London and Damon Runyon.

"Jack London because of the times was racist," Tyson said. "He used bad words like dusky and negro and this and that. But he always used those words with greatness. 'The nigger was MAGNIFICENT,'" said Tyson with a flourish of his arms.
"I never looked at it as a racist remark, because of the time at the turn of the century ... but he said it with admiration."
Tyson, who has three daughters -- Gina, 7, Rayna, 9 months, and Michael Lorna, 6 -- was asked if he changes diapers.
Not often, he said. "I'm capable of doing it. But if I don't have to do it I'm not gonna do it."
The fighter said he realises he eventually has to tell his daughters of his past, which includes reform school, law suits and three years in prison for rape.

"I gotta tell them what I used to do was bad. I gotta explain to them even though it was bad why I did it because I wasn't a smart guy back them," said the man who was once quoted by a former friend as saying Tyson once boasted he slept with several women in one night, and he liked to hurt women when he had sex with them.

He said he has to tell his daughters: "I'm trying to stop you guys from making the same mistake as Daddy did, so I got to go through that whole scenario, you know, I'm not really looking forward to it. But it's something that has to be done."
One of his proudest accomplishments, he said, was that his daughters would be the first generation of Tysons who won't be on welfare.
"To think that my daughter is not going to be on welfare, to me that's fly (great)."
